title: Promissory Notes: Boring Name, Sexy Deal Tool

 Promissory Notes: Boring Name, Sexy Deal Tool
Hi Sara,
If you’re buying or selling a business, you’ve probably met our friend: the promissory note.
Sounds dull. It’s anything but.
A promissory note is a promise to pay. Groundbreaking, I know. But before you tune out, here’s why it matters: when used right, it can make the difference between a deadlocked deal and one that gets across the finish line.
Here’s what you need to know—without needing a law degree:
You want $1.2 million for your business. The buyer’s stuck on $1 million. Enter: the promissory note. That extra $200K? It can live in a note, payable if the business performs post-closing. It’s called a retention adjustment, and it’s basically the deal version of “let’s see who’s right.”
But don’t stop there.
You can slice and dice a note like a Vegas card shark. $500K note? Make $50K of it the SBA-required “equity injection” (hello, 24-month standby). Carve the rest into separate notes with different terms. The bank cares about how the equity portion of the Note is structured, but may have different (and more lenient) thoughts on the other parts.
Why I Like Notes More Than Earn-Outs if I’m the Buyer
Earn-outs are needy. They involve escrow agents, agreements, arguments, and fees. Notes? You just draft them, sign them, and boom—you’re off to the races. They’re elegant. They’re manageable. And they don’t come with a customer service line.
If you’re a busy business owner—and most of my clients are—this kind of simplicity matters. Notes let you build in conditional payments without the administrative circus of a full-blown earn-out. We love that.
*But ON THE OTHER HAND, if I’m the seller, I certainly like the fact that my money is sitting in an escrow account somewhere. 
One Last Note (Get It?)
Don't treat notes like a monolith. Be strategic. Use multiple notes. Tailor the terms. And above all: stop pretending like “standard terms” are your only option. You can (and should) get creative.

To smarter structuring,
Sara Sharp
Partner, SK&S Law Group
